summary: Specifies two forward error correction schemes, LDPC Staircase and LDPC Triangle, for reliably delivering data objects over a channel where packets are either received intact or lost. They use low density parity check codes with large blocks. It is a standards-track specification.

plainLanguage.summary: When sending a puzzle by mail, you add some extra spare pieces. If a few get lost, the receiver can still rebuild the picture. LDPC is a way to make those spares.

questions: forward error correction for packet loss
how does forward error correction recover lost packets
what is the fec payload id
subtitle: Two large-block codes that add repair packets so receivers can rebuild an object even when some packets are lost.

tldr.problem: When packets can be lost but never arrive corrupted, a sender needs a way to let receivers recover missing data without asking for retransmissions.
tldr.mechanism: LDPC-Staircase and LDPC-Triangle build a parity check matrix of XOR equations from a shared pseudo-random generator, produce repair symbols from the source symbols, and let the receiver solve the equations to recover what was lost.
tldr.outcome: They are Fully-Specified FEC Schemes with FEC Encoding IDs 3 and 4. The RFC leaves the decoding technique to the codec developer, because interoperability does not depend on it.

today: RFC 5170 is a Proposed Standard from June 2008, and the unit metadata shows no RFC obsoleting or updating it. It defines FEC Encoding IDs 3 and 4 in the "ietf:rmt:fec:encoding" name-space.

sections.title: Large Block FEC for Lossy Channels
sections.content:
RFC 5170 describes two Fully-Specified Forward Error Correction (FEC) Schemes, LDPC-Staircase and LDPC-Triangle. They are meant for the reliable delivery of data objects over a packet erasure channel: a path where each packet is either received without corruption or dropped.

Both are large block codes in the sense of RFC 3453, so they can work efficiently on source blocks of several tens of thousands of source symbols. They are also systematic: the encoding symbols include the original source symbols as well as the repair symbols. LDPC-Staircase uses FEC Encoding ID 3 and LDPC-Triangle uses FEC Encoding ID 4.

Both rely on a parity check matrix, which defines relationships between the encoding symbols. The decoder uses them to reconstruct the original k source symbols when some are missing. Sender and receiver must use the same matrix, so the information needed to build it travels in the FEC Object Transmission Information.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender mails the real puzzle pieces plus some spare pieces. Both sides agree on a recipe for how the spares are made, so the receiver can use them to fill in for lost pieces.

sections.title: Symbols, Blocks and Code Rate
sections.content:
A source symbol is a unit of data used in encoding. An encoding symbol is a unit generated by encoding, and a repair symbol is an encoding symbol that is not a source symbol. A source block is a block of k source symbols that are encoded together, and n is the number of encoding symbols generated for it.

The code rate is the ratio k/n. A rate close to 1 means few repair symbols were produced. An Encoding Symbol Group is a set of G encoding symbols sent in one packet, and a packet holds either only source symbols or only repair symbols.

Other notations used throughout: L is the object length in bytes, E is the symbol length in bytes, B is the maximum source block length in symbols, N is the number of source blocks, and max_n is the maximum number of encoding symbols generated for any source block.
sections.plainLanguage: A symbol is one piece of the puzzle. The code rate tells you how many real pieces there are compared with all pieces, spares included.

sections.title: The FEC Payload ID
sections.content:
Each packet carries exactly one FEC Payload ID, made of two fields. The Source Block Number (12 bits) says which source block of the object the symbols come from, with a maximum of 2^12 blocks per object and numbering starting at 0. The Encoding Symbol ID (20 bits) says which encoding symbols of that block the packet carries, with a maximum of 2^20 per block.

ESI values 0 to k-1 identify source symbols and the remaining values identify repair symbols. When a packet holds several symbols, the Payload ID names only the first one, and the others are worked out from it.
sections.plainLanguage: Each package has a label saying which puzzle section it belongs to and which piece number comes first inside.

sections.title: FEC Object Transmission Information
sections.content:
The FEC Object Transmission Information (FEC OTI) tells the receiver how the object was encoded. The mandatory element is the FEC Encoding ID, 3 for Staircase or 4 for Triangle. Four common elements MUST be defined: Transfer-Length (L), Encoding-Symbol-Length (E), Maximum-Source-Block-Length (B) and Max-Number-of-Encoding-Symbols (max_n), which is at most 2^20.

Three scheme-specific elements MUST also be defined. N1m3 is an integer from 0 (default) to 7, and the target number of 1s per column on the left of the matrix is N1 = N1m3 + 3. G is from 1 (default) to 31 symbols per packet. The PRNG seed is a 32-bit unsigned integer from 1 to 0x7FFFFFFE.

The maximum transfer length is 2^12 * B * E. For example, with B = 2^19 and E = 1024 bytes it is 2^41 bytes (2 TB). The RFC shows two encodings: the EXT_FTI header extension, used by protocols such as ALC and NORM, and XML attributes in a FLUTE File Delivery Table instance, where the scheme-specific part is Base64 encoded. It does not say when either should be used.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender sends a small instruction sheet: how big the pieces are, how many spares there are, and a secret starting number for the recipe. Without it the receiver could not rebuild the same recipe.

sections.title: Choosing Parameters and Partitioning
sections.content:
The sender first picks B, E and G, then splits the object into N source blocks using the block partitioning algorithm of RFC 5052. The first I blocks have A_large source symbols and the rest have A_small. Each symbol is E bytes, except perhaps the last. Suggested algorithms exist for B, E, G and max_n, but a sender MAY use others because the results travel in the FEC OTI.

B is limited by the code rate. For rates from 1/2 up to but not including 1, B is at most 2^19 = 524,288 symbols. For rates from 1/4 up to but not including 1/2 it is 2^18 = 262,144. E is normally chosen as large as possible so a single-symbol packet stays just below the path MTU. Grouping several symbols per packet saves header overhead, but then each lost packet loses G symbols.

The number of encoding symbols for a block is fixed by the n-algorithm, which sender and receiver MUST both use: n = floor(k * max_n / B).

The random number generator MUST be the Park-Miller "minimal standard" PRNG, with A = 7^5 = 16807 and M = 2^31 - 1. As a check, with seed 1 the 10,000th value returned MUST be 1043618065.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender cuts the big file into sections, picks how big each piece is, and decides how many spares to make. Both sides use the same random-number recipe so they build exactly the same spare pieces.

sections.title: Staircase and Triangle Matrices
sections.content:
Each block is encoded and decoded on its own. The parity check matrix is a system of linear equations, with XOR as the basic operator, and an entry 1 at row i, column j means the symbol with ESI j appears in equation i. The left side (columns 0 to k-1) covers source symbols and is built by the same left_matrix_init() function for both schemes. The two schemes differ only in the right side, which covers repair symbols.

In LDPC-Staircase, the right side has an identity diagonal plus a second diagonal below it. Each repair symbol is the sum of the source symbols in its equation plus the previous repair symbol, so encoding MUST proceed in repair symbol order. In LDPC-Triangle, the right side also gets randomly placed extra 1s below the staircase, and each repair symbol is the sum of the source and lower-numbered repair symbols in its equation.

Decoding means solving n-k linear equations to recover the k source symbols. The RFC describes a simple algorithm: if an equation has only one unknown, its value follows, and substituting it can reveal others. Gaussian elimination can recover from fewer known symbols but costs more CPU. The RFC recommends no particular decoder, since interoperability does not depend on it. It also notes that shuffling parity symbols before sending is usually recommended, because sending them in sequence is suboptimal.
sections.plainLanguage: Each spare piece is made by mixing together a few other pieces. When one piece goes missing, you find a mixing rule where it is the only unknown and solve for it, then repeat. The two versions of the code just mix pieces in slightly different patterns.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC treats FEC as a building block independent of any content delivery protocol and discusses added threats: access to confidential content, corruption of the object, and attacks that make decoding expensive. For confidentiality, encryption of the whole object before encoding or per packet (for example IPsec/ESP) is RECOMMENDED when it is a concern. This is not related to FEC itself.

For corruption, integrity and sender authentication can be applied to the whole object (a digital signature, where a receiver cannot tell which symbols are bad) or to packets (per-packet signatures, a group MAC with a shared key, or TESLA). If there is any concern about object corruption, at least one of these techniques is RECOMMENDED.

The FEC OTI itself can be attacked: changing B, for example, changes the block partitioning and prevents decoding. Integrity of the FEC OTI is therefore RECOMMENDED, and EXT_FTI packets SHOULD be protected by a per-packet technique.
sections.plainLanguage: A sneaky person could swap in fake pieces or change the instruction sheet so the puzzle cannot be rebuilt. Locking the pieces and the sheet with a signed seal prevents that.
